summary: Vitals Console is a health tool that helps an astronaut check their own health when help from Earth is slow to arrive. NASA describes a Mars round trip as roughly three years, and its research papers cite signal delays of up to 24 minutes each way, so crews can’t just wait for a flight surgeon. Our console tracks eight indicators: heart rate, blood pressure, glucose, temperature, sleep, mood and exercise. A fingertip camera reading can measure pulse. A clickable body map and color-coded charts show status at a glance. Machine-learning and statistical methods learn each astronaut’s own baseline, catch slow drift before a reading turns red, forecast trends, and spot patterns across NASA’s five hazards. When something looks wrong, the app writes a one-message report for the flight surgeon, gives a “while you wait” plan, and shows a delay clock. Quests, ranks and badges keep the routine engaging. It matters because longer missions need astronauts who can act safely on their own.
details:
Astronauts log their numbers in a daily check-in by typing them in or reading their pulse with the phone camera. They cover the lens and flash with a fingertip for 15 seconds. The app averages the red brightness of each video frame, removes slow drift, finds the heartbeats, and turns the median gap between beats into beats per minute.

The first seven days become the astronaut’s personal baseline. Then the app uses machine learning to do the following:

smooths the readings to flag drift away from their own normal

forecasts seven days ahead

scores how unusual the day is overall against a 95% statistical limit

checks four patterns that link NASA hazards to the indicators, such as isolation strain and cardiovascular deconditioning

estimates next-day risk, detects when a change began, and shows how sleep and exercise affect the next day

A clickable body map and color-coded status show where attention is needed. The Report tab writes a structured message for the flight surgeon and shows a delay clock. It also gives a checklist of safe actions to take while waiting.

Astronauts get early, personal warnings instead of one-size-fits-all ranges. Plain explanations tell them why each measurement matters and how to take it. The one-message report saves round trips when every reply takes close to an hour.

We want crews on long missions to be able to spot problems early and make a sensible first response without Earth. The same ideas could help people in remote communities, on expeditions, and in telehealth, where care is far away.

Most health trackers compare you with a population average. Ours learns each astronaut’s own normal and is designed around communication delay, which is one of NASA’s five hazards. The body map, pulse reader, quests and cross-hazard patterns are woven into one console that looks like real mission software.

We used HTML, CSS, and plain JavaScript.

We considered the usability of our app for non-experts in the field so even if the astronauts don't know much, they can still use the app.
projectRefs: Remote healthcare in space and on Earth
